newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FEATURE-Violent youth rebel in Singapore.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Violent youth rebel in Singapore.

text.p: Singapore has a reputation for discipline, hard work and abiding by the law but a growing minority of youths is rebelling and turning to violent crime.
Teenage street hooligans and girl gangs are featuring more prominently in the city-state's crime records despite strict laws and stiff punishments.
Since the beginning of 1997 police have recorded 148 riots, up from 105 for the same period in 1996.
About 2,000 youths turn up in court each year, and around 10 percent of these are in gangs, according to the National Youth Council (NYC).
"We have deployed mobile police posts in trouble spots. It has turned the tide but the problem is a long-term one," said NYC director Lee How Sheng.
Lee said today's street gangs were not usually involved in organised crime but regularly fought with rival gangs.
These often led to injury and sometimes murder.
Groups of youths, some sporting tattoos and clean-shaven heads, mill on the streets around the city's nightspots. They smoke, drink and consume fashionable new drugs such as ecstasy.
STREET HOOLIGANISM ON THE RISE
The Singapore River strip, with a run of 21 bars, has been targeted by teenagers, students, national servicemen and bikers as one of the best places to hang out.
But recent violence along the strip between youths has rung alarm bells in the city-state, raising fears that it may taint the image of the city and put off tourists.
Tolerance for unruly youth is traditionally limited. The state that prides itself on being clean and disciplined demonstrated that when American teenager Michael Fay was caned for vandalism in 1994.
Studies have shown a consistent increase in the number of youths arrested for offences related to gangs.
A recent survey of 150 gang members showed that a significant proportion were males between 13 and 15. Students formed about 81.4 percent of the youth gang members and many were low achievers.

Youths with their loose street clothing may not be hiding guns in their baggy jeans, as Singapore has strict laws on dangerous arms. But they have been known to use knives, knuckle dusters and rattan poles to maim and kill, police say.
In March, in what appeared to be a racially motivated incident, several Malay teenage boys attacked a Chinese leaving him dead with five stab wounds.
LACK OF HOME SUPPORT BLAMED
Social workers say today's rebellious teenagers are turning to gangs partly because of a lack of social cohesion.

They say the rising cost of living in Singapore, which is one of the world's wealthiest countries with an annual per capita income of over US$24,000, has pressured parents to work, leaving them little time to spend with their kids.
"Teenagers need a sense of belonging. At this age, if they can't find identity at home they find it among their peers," said Jade Lee, a social worker.

"When the state plays nanny and forces youngsters home earlier, it lets irresponsible parents off the hook from disciplining their offspring," journalist Raoul Le Blond wrote in a recent editorial in Singapore's Sunday Times.
Singapore is trying a number of responses to gangs.
Some Singaporeans have suggested teenage curfews to curb delinquency but this idea has been criticised.
Cafe and restaurant owner Y.F. Wan said curfews did not solve the problem of displacement and a lack of discipline in an achievement-oriented society.
"The fundamental root of the problem is that parents have no time for their kids," he said, noting parents who work all day sometimes appease their guilt by giving money.
"A gang leader provides leadership, and under that leadership they will succumb to anything. Fights and weapons are a symbol of power and invincibility," he said.
The city-state already metes out stiff punishments ranging from caning and long jail terms for many crimes and has the death penalty for drug trafficking and murder.
Pubs and dance clubs now work closely with the police to control drug and alcohol abuse, often a prelude to fights.
"We frisk all the men, search bags of men and women, use TV cameras and conduct spot urine checks on our own staff," said Andrew Ing, marketing manager of Zouk, a big dance club.
But he said it was not so acceptable for doormen to pick and choose the crowd as they often did in New York and London.
"People in Asia don't understand. They think they're not good enough and get offended," Ing said.
